records.our_prose: Cantaloupe does not need a lot of nitrogen, and too much gives you big leafy vines but fewer, less sweet melons. Mix a fertilizer that is lower in nitrogen, like a 5-10-10, into the soil before planting, then give the plants a little nitrogen before the vines start to run and again after the flowers bloom. Once the melons start to form, stop pushing nitrogen so the plant puts its energy into growing sweet fruit instead of more leaves.

records.our_prose: Cantaloupe is a moderate feeder that wants more phosphorus and potassium than nitrogen, since excess nitrogen drives leafy vine at the expense of fruit set and sugar. Work a lower-nitrogen complete fertilizer such as 5-10-10 into the bed before planting (Clemson suggests about 30 pounds per 1,000 square feet), then side-dress with a nitrogen source before the vines start to run, and again lightly after bloom as fruit develops. Ease off nitrogen once fruit has set so the plant pours its energy into sizing and sweetening the melons rather than growing more vine. Pair feeding with even moisture, because the nutrients only help a plant that is not also drought-stressed.
source_names: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

records.our_prose: Try not to grow cantaloupe or its relatives (cucumbers, melons, squash) in the same spot more than once every 3 years, and wait longer if you have had wilt or leaf disease. Moving them around the garden helps avoid a buildup of soil and debris diseases. Note that this does not stop bacterial wilt, which comes from beetles, not the soil. Clean up old vines at the end of the season too.

records.source_context: Do not till bark or wood chip mulches into the soil close to plants, as they will tie up nitrogen as they decompose. Synthetic mulches should be removed and discarded at the end of the season or when they are no longer useful as mulches. Organic mulch materials can be turned into the soil with a spade or rototiller or placed in your compost pile.

records.our_prose: Cantaloupe does best in deep, well-drained, light soil, with sandy loams and loamy sands the classic choice because they warm quickly in spring and drain freely, which this heat-loving, warm-season vine rewards with earlier, sweeter fruit. Work a few inches of compost or well-rotted manure into the bed before planting, but go easier on high-nitrogen amendments than you would for leafy crops, since too much nitrogen pushes vine at the expense of fruit set and sugar. Many growers plant on low, wide hills or raised mounds, which warm faster, drain better, and lift the crown and developing fruit off wet ground. Heavy clay holds water and stays cold, slowing growth and inviting Fusarium wilt and fruit rot, so amend it generously and build mounds, or grow on sandier ground.

records.our_prose: About 1 to 2 inches of water a week is a good target, more while the plant is flowering and the melons are growing.
records.source_context: Drip irrigation works well as it provides water directly to the root zone and reduces the wetting of the foliage, which can promote disease issues and weed growth (both of which are difficult to deal with when growing melons). During dry weather, irrigate by applying 1 to 2 inches of water every 7 to 10 days. Irrigate in the early morning to reduce foliage diseases.

records.our_prose: Aim for about 1 to 2 inches of water per week, more in heat or on sandy soil, delivered deeply and less often rather than in light daily sprinkles. Cantaloupe is deep-rooted and the fruit is largely water, so steady moisture through vining and fruit sizing is essential, but the plant also wants a dry finish to sweeten.
